title: The Missing Index
summary: Order history pages time out. The database has three replicas and is still on fire, because every query scans the whole table.
scenario: An online store serves 2,000 requests per second, 90% of them customers opening "My orders". The query is SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?.
The orders table has 80 million rows and no index on customer_id, so every request reads the entire table. The team already added two read replicas. It barely helped.
Make order pages fast and reliable without blowing the budget.

functional: Look up orders by customer_id in an 80M-row table
nonFunctional: Average latency at or below 65 ms

objectives.label: Average latency at or below 65 ms

hints: Run it and select the Orders DB. Notice the "no index" badge and what the bottleneck message says about how reads are served.

Without an index, finding one customer's orders means reading all 80 million rows. More replicas just means more machines doing full scans. A cache won't save you either: only 20% of reads hit popular keys.
Select the Orders DB and set Indexes to Standard. Read capacity jumps 5× and latency drops 4×. One setting, no extra cost.
explanation: An index is a sorted lookup structure (usually a B-tree) on one or more columns. With an index on customer_id, the database jumps straight to that customer's rows: O(log n) instead of scanning all n rows.

Missing indexes are one of the most common causes of production database outages, and they hide well: on a small dev database the full scan is instant, and the problem only appears at real data sizes.
Scaling hardware around a missing index is expensive and only linear: here you would need about 14 replicas of full scans to match what one index does for free.

Indexes aren't free either. Every INSERT and UPDATE must also update every index, and they take disk space. Index the columns you filter and sort on, and check slow-query logs (EXPLAIN shows a "Seq Scan" when an index is missing).
